channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] The Coast Guard and FBI boarded two US-bound energy tankers after foreign cyber actors compromised their networks
item.category: Top Story
item.description: A joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement reported on 16 September confirms two offshore security boardings in the Gulf of Mexico, on 21 and 24 August. They were carried out to ensure the integrity of the vessels’ operational and information technology systems, after indications that the networks of both ships had been compromised. The Coast Guard told The Record the networks “were compromised by foreign cyber actors.” The boarding parties combined Coast Guard law enforcement, a vessel inspector and Cyber Protection Team members with FBI Cyber Action Team operators. The strongest on-record finding comes from Rear Adm. Amy Grable, commander of Coast Guard Cyber Command. She told CBS News that investigators “did find malicious cyber activity” aboard the VL Prosperity, where the team spent about four days. SecurityWeek quotes her as saying nothing found during the inspection suggested the tanker was unsafe to operate. Her concern about IT systems connected to propulsion and navigation was stated as a risk, not as a finding. The VL Prosperity is a 333 m Liberian-flagged crude supertanker managed by HMM Ocean Service. It loaded at Sidi Kerir, Egypt, bound for Galveston, Texas, and the compromise is placed at around 7 August near the Strait of Gibraltar. HMM Ocean Service says the Coast Guard has cleared it for normal operations. The second vessel has not been named by either agency and is reported to be an LNG carrier. Both agencies report no operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews or environmental impacts. Officials told Bloomberg the hackers did not appear to have taken control of the ships. Bloomberg also reports, citing unnamed officials, that the Coast Guard, FBI and CISA are tracking cyber threats against nearly 20 vessels worldwide. The Coast Guard has asked for advance notice if any of those ships plans to enter a US port. Two further claims originate with Iranian state media (Mehr): that attackers took control of navigation, propulsion and cargo systems, and that one ship lost communications for about 30 hours. TechCrunch repeated them on 18 September as “reportedly”, and no US official has confirmed them. No attribution has been made and no group has claimed responsibility. The crew of a separate LNG carrier has since reported a suspected cyber incident; that case is covered below and is not confirmed. - Joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement quoted by CyberScoop and The Record; Rear Adm. Amy Grable to CBS News and SecurityWeek; vessel detail and the nearly-20-vessel tracking via gCaptain citing Bloomberg; TechCrunch (18 Sep) for the “reportedly” framing of Iranian claims - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; publicly confirmed 16 Sep 2026; claims re-checked against reporting of 16–18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] An LNG carrier with a US cargo lost access to some onboard control systems and its crew suspects a cyberattack, though the cause is officially undetermined
item.category: Incident — Suspected, cause undetermined: LNG carrier control systems
item.description: Bloomberg reported on 18 September, in a story republished by gCaptain, that the crew of the Vivit Africa LNG lost access to some internal control systems in early September in the Mediterranean. The crew reported a suspected cyberattack to Korean Register, the vessel’s technical and safety adviser, and Korean Register says its investigation is ongoing. The ship is South Korean-owned, operated by H-Line Shipping and on long-term time charter to Vitol; The Next Web reports it as Liberia-flagged. It had loaded at Cameron LNG in Louisiana for the Adriatic LNG terminal near Rovigo, Italy. It abandoned that destination and headed west towards Algeciras, Spain. The Italian Coast Guard described a malfunction in the systems that monitor cargo parameters, said the cause had not been identified, and said it intervened solely for navigation safety. Kongsberg Maritime supplies equipment aboard, which Bloomberg describes as positioning, navigation and propulsion technology. Kongsberg says it is too early to draw conclusions about the cause or any security implications. There are no indications of who might be responsible. Bloomberg counts this as the third tanker in about a month tied to suspected cyber activity, after the two vessels the Coast Guard and FBI boarded, but nothing published connects the cases. Treat it as what it is so far: a crew report of a suspected attack and a cargo-monitoring malfunction, not a confirmed intrusion. - Bloomberg, republished by gCaptain, with Italian Coast Guard, Korean Register and Kongsberg Maritime statements; corroborated by Investing.com and The Next Web - Incident early Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026; Korean Register investigation ongoing

item.title: [Critical] Malaysia’s Port of Tanjung Pelepas has resumed container operations after a cyber incident halted its terminal
item.category: Incident — Container terminal operations, recovered
item.description: The Port of Tanjung Pelepas said on 15 September that container terminal operations had resumed, with system recovery advancing steadily, after a cybersecurity incident hit its terminal operating systems. The incident was detected at 23:34 local time on 9 September; PTP isolated the affected systems and suspended container handling as a precaution, processed gate-ins manually from the evening of 10 September and began a controlled, phased restart the same day. A Maersk spokesperson — the port is a Maersk and MMC joint venture — confirmed the incident to The Loadstar and said some vessels might be delayed; the Maersk Hanoi deviated by about ten hours, while a Kuehne+Nagel summary of Lloyd’s List reporting noted no significant queues. PTP says there is no evidence of unauthorised access to customer data. No attacker, initial access vector or verified ransomware claim has been disclosed, and sources differ on how long handling stopped, from several hours to about a day. PTP handled more than 14m TEU in 2025 and anchors the Gemini network of Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd. It remains the clearest recent demonstration that a terminal does not need its cranes touched to stop. - Port of Tanjung Pelepas statements to WorldCargo News and an A.P. Moller-Maersk statement to The Loadstar; Kuehne+Nagel summary of Lloyd’s List reporting - Incident detected 9 Sep 2026; phased restart began 10 Sep 2026; operations resumed per PTP 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A state administration refused to pay and its infrastructure vulnerability analyses were published
item.category: Incident — Public-authority breach publishes infrastructure risk documentation
item.description: Rhysida released data taken from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set is around 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files and, alongside personnel and payroll records, is reported to include vulnerability analyses of the city’s water supply and plaintext credentials for municipal systems including a building atlas, a payments database and administrator accounts. Berlin’s account has data leaving from 7 August through around 12 August, with affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. Most US port authorities are public bodies subject to the same dynamics: the facility security assessment, the new MTSA cyber assessment, terminal drawings and crane and gate system documentation frequently sit on a state or municipal network run by someone other than the port’s own security team. - Berlin state administration statements — reported by Help Net Security and Security Affairs - Breach and refusal to pay reported 1 Sep 2026; data published by the actor 4 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Undocumented cellular modems in ZPMC ship-to-shore cranes — confirmed hardware, assessed intent, no observed use
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Supply chain, ship-to-shore crane control
item.description: This is standing context rather than new reporting: US Maritime Administration Advisory 2026-007 was issued on 24 April 2026 and remains in force to 21 October, and the distinction inside the crane supply-chain problem is the part worth carrying into a risk register. What is confirmed is physical: US Coast Guard and congressional inspections found undocumented cellular modems fitted to cranes built by Shanghai Zhenhua Heavy Industries, wired with direct access to the crane industrial controllers and bypassing the port firewalls that are meant to sit in front of them. What is assessed rather than observed is the consequence — an intelligence judgement that those modems could be used to monitor crane activity or disable cranes during a crisis. No such use has been reported anywhere, and this is structural exposure rather than an incident. The reason it still matters is population. ZPMC builds an estimated 72–78 per cent of the world’s ship-to-shore cranes and roughly 80 per cent of those installed in US and European ports, so the exposure is most of the fleet rather than an unlucky subset. MARAD Advisory 2026-007 names ZPMC cranes alongside China’s LOGINK logistics-data platform and Nuctech scanning systems as foreign adversarial technology risks to US port infrastructure, and asks facilities to apply access control, network segmentation and monitoring and offline backups, and to report anomalies to the Coast Guard, CISA and the FBI. Ports are responding with retrofits — removing the foreign modems, replacing crane software, separating crane OT networks — supported by an executive order and more than $20bn in federal loans, with Konecranes and a revived Mitsui E&S North American line named as alternative suppliers. - US Maritime Administration Advisory 2026-007, which names ZPMC cranes, LOGINK and Nuctech directly; inspection and retrofit details from earlier public reporting - MARAD Advisory 2026-007 issued 24 Apr 2026 and in force through 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Port, terminal and logistics operators sit inside the business-services and transport categories driving this record. For maritime the relevant point is that a terminal does not need its cranes encrypted to stop — losing the terminal operating system, gate systems or EDI is enough. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For ships and terminals the argument lands naturally, because the sector already thinks in terms of consequence and redundancy. The question it asks is whether the engineered fallbacks — manual steering, local crane control, mechanical stops — are genuinely independent of the digital systems they are meant to back up. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The monitoring problem nobody wants to say out loud: you cannot scan a running engine room
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, monitoring practice
item.description: An analysis published by Cybersecurity Insiders on 12 September sets out the visibility gap in shipboard OT in plainer terms than most vendor material manages. Propulsion, steering, ballast, power-management, cargo and navigation systems are increasingly networked, while much of the equipment is ageing, vendor-specific and connected intermittently over satellite. The argument the piece makes is one many fleet security teams have reached independently: active interrogation — the scanning and polling that works on a corporate network — is not safe against safety-critical control systems at sea, so passive, non-intrusive monitoring with local collection and shore-based analysis is the realistic path to continuous anomaly detection. It also flags the exposure growing fastest: remote maintenance, satellite links, autonomous shipping, electrification and automated ports. Treat this as informed practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting — it describes no attack and names no victim — but it maps directly onto what IMO and IACS now expect operators to be able to demonstrate. - Cybersecurity Insiders analysis — surfaced via the Viakoo daily OT briefing. Practitioner analysis, not incident reporting; no primary-source incident underlies it - Published 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Google says a criminal group ran an entire credential-harvesting campaign with autonomous agents in under six hours
item.category: Threat Intel — Autonomous multi-agent intrusion tooling
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor executed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign end to end in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework — the agents, not operators, carried the campaign through its stages. GTIG separately observed actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and running unauthorised AI workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants. Its assessment is blunt: assume every threat actor is using AI to some degree. For ports, terminals and vessel operators the practical consequence is timing. Credential phishing against shoreside schedulers, agents, chandlers and crewing staff is the standard first move against a maritime estate, and a six-hour campaign lands entirely inside a single watch — often one with satellite latency and no responder aboard. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting — via The Hacker News - Published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Fire Ant turns routers and authentication servers into listening posts inside critical-infrastructure networks
item.category: Threat Intel — State-nexus compromise of network and authentication infrastructure
item.description: Sygnia published research on 30 August showing the China-nexus group it tracks as Fire Ant has moved beyond VMware hypervisors into network infrastructure itself: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts inside a large interconnected estate. Router implants suppressed chosen syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and offered interactive shells that logged nothing; on TACACS the actor hooked the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as logins were approved. Sygnia observed scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks, without confirming compromise there. Ports and terminals should read this as a warning about the layer they examine least. Terminal operating systems, crane and gate networks and shore-to-ship links all traverse routers a third party maintains — and the audit trail a Coast Guard incident report would rest on comes from those same devices. - Sygnia research publication and press release — corroborated by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Cybersecurity Dive and SC Media - Sygnia published 30 Aug 2026; wider reporting 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
item.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a terminal or fleet operator this lands on the response side: shore-side monitoring is often business-hours, and a vessel in passage has satellite latency and no local responder at all. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect the terminal — and a three-month planning horizon
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. For a terminal the hard step is the first one, because the dependency map runs outside the fence — customs and manifest feeds, carrier systems, the terminal operating system’s cloud components. North Carolina Ports demonstrated the graduated version in August by moving cargo processing to manual while vessel work continued. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months of isolated operation is the part worth testing against your own manual fallbacks, which are usually scoped for days. - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] AI-assisted exploit porting: a working PLC exploit moved to a second controller model in hours
item.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For terminals and vessels the point is portability. Cargo handling, ballast and power-management controllers come in close model families, and an exploit proven on one variant is now cheaper to move to its siblings than most risk registers assume. - Forescout Vedere Labs research reported by SecurityWeek - Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques. For ports, terminals and shipowners the relevant line is the one about assumption: the NCSC tells organisations not to believe their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure comes from misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. Maritime OT is unusually good at generating all three — crane and straddle-carrier control systems commissioned by an OEM and still reachable over a vendor support link, terminal operating system interfaces, shore-power and bunkering controls, and vessel systems whose remote maintenance path was set up for a class survey and never withdrawn. The alert also maps closely onto IACS UR E26 and E27 expectations already binding on newbuilds. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ISE carries a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass exploited as a zero-day — and ISE is often what separates port IT from port OT
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC scored CVSS 10.0. An unauthenticated remote attacker can reach an API endpoint with insufficient authentication and bypass the web-based management interface. Cisco states plainly that its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions of ISE and ISE-PIC are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There is no workaround — the mitigation is infrastructure access control lists restricting management traffic. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure targeting has been claimed. The maritime relevance is architectural rather than product-specific: ISE is frequently the 802.1X and network access control policy engine that decides which ports, which contractors and which vendor laptops are allowed onto terminal, gate and crane network segments, and which remote-access sessions reach the industrial DMZ. Administrative control of that policy engine is administrative control of the boundary your Cybersecurity Plan says exists. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — version detail via BleepingComputer - Cisco advisory published 16 Sep 2026; KEV addition 16 Sep 2026, due 19 Sep 2026; further reporting 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s six ICS advisories of 17 September contain nothing maritime — which is worth recording rather than padding
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no maritime product
item.description: CISA released six industrial control system advisories on Thursday 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -06, covering Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy’s FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5, and ABB Ability Edgenius. The highest confirmed score in the batch is CVE-2026-15688 in Mitsubishi GX Works3, an authentication algorithm weakness affecting all versions, scored CVSS 8.8 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, with CISA listing Critical Manufacturing. The Bransys ELD advisory covers hardcoded MQTT and FTP credentials and cleartext transmission, highest score CVSS 7.5, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54 — electronic logging devices are commercial-trucking equipment, so the Transportation Systems label on it should not be read across to vessels or terminals. Severity scores and the CISA sector lists for the Hitachi Energy, Schneider and ABB advisories could not be verified at the time of this edition and are deliberately not quoted here; check the advisory pages directly before acting on them. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, ICSA-26-211-07 covering the Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN communication protocol was updated on 17 September with eight newly affected products. For a marine estate the practical filter is narrow: Modicon controllers and NetBotz environmental monitoring do turn up in terminal plant and port facilities, so run the inventory check; nothing in this batch touches shipboard systems. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -06 and the ICSA-26-211-07 update — verified against the CISA CSAF repository pull request for 17 Sep, which was truncated for four of the six advisories - Advisories released 17 Sep 2026; scores for ICSA-26-260-03 to -06 unverified at time of writing

item.title: [High] Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard carries two hard-coded key flaws scored 9.0 and 9.1 — the risk depends on how it was installed
item.category: Advisory — Vessel software, hard-coded cryptographic keys
item.description: CISA’s 15 September ICS advisory batch includes ICSA-26-258-02 for Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard version 5.07.0923.01, used in the maritime transportation sector. It covers two hard-coded cryptographic key weaknesses, both CWE-321: CVE-2026-81855 (CVSS 9.1), a hard-coded client authentication key in the robot testing framework, and CVE-2026-78225 (CVSS 9.0), a hard-coded server key in the deployer-ng Update Controller. Per the advisory, exploitation could let an attacker deliver unauthorised updates, execute code, or extract credentials to impersonate a privileged client. Wärtsilä states the flaws are not exploitable when the product is installed as recommended, and a patch is available by contacting Wärtsilä. CISA lists Transportation Systems as the affected sector and reports no known public exploitation targeting these vulnerabilities. The advisory has since been confirmed against CISA’s machine-readable CSAF file, so the version and score detail above is settled; this remains the only shipboard-software advisory in the 15 September batch. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-02, verified against the CISA CSAF machine-readable file - Advisory released 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and port, terminal and vessel teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Terminal operating system integrations, crane and gate automation scripts, EDI and port-community interfaces and vessel fleet-management tooling are routinely versioned in self-hosted GitLab at port authorities, terminal operators and ship managers. Unauthenticated file reads expose the secrets that connect shore IT to crane, gate and cargo systems. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to twelve flaws — older CVEs, a patched device, and an inventory check rather than an emergency
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to twelve vulnerabilities: nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, with CVSS scores reported in the 5.3 to 8.5 range. Nozomi demonstrated that several can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow telemetry manipulation, alarm suppression, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement. Two points of framing matter. First, this is not a new critical advisory: the first part of the research, published 10 September, described four PROFINET DCP memory-corruption flaws each scored CVSS 5.3 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads — and the underlying CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under ICSA-25-135-18. What happened on 15 September was CISA updating that 2025 advisory to add the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and the vendor fixes, not a new disclosure. Second, Siemens has already patched: affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1, fixed in V4.0 HF0 and later. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. The CVE identifiers carry 2025 prefixes despite the 2026 publication, so verify them against Siemens’ own security advisory before using them in a change record. Where terminals or vessels use the LPE9403 as an edge gateway between PROFINET-connected equipment and shore-side monitoring, root on that gateway means the SCADA view of the equipment behind it can no longer be trusted. - Nozomi Networks Labs research (parts one and two) and Siemens ProductCERT — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Underlying CVEs disclosed May 2025 (ICSA-25-135-18); research published 10 and 18 Sep 2026; CISA advisory updated 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch wave lands on the controllers and relays behind terminal power, cranes and shore systems
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch cycle
item.description: Schneider Electric and Siemens shipped their September fixes on 8 September, and two items reach directly into port and vessel estates. Schneider’s most severe is an authentication flaw in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the M580 family runs conveyor lines, bulk handling, pump rooms and shore-power switching at terminals across the sector. Alongside it are high-severity fixes for the PowerLogic T300 RTU, formerly Easergy T300, and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September, headlined by fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays where a session-identifier leak allows authentication bypass. Aveva patched four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key; CISA formalised that set on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01 — CVE-2026-81821 and CVE-2026-81822, both CVSS 8.4, alongside CVE-2026-81823 at 5.3 and CVE-2026-81824 at 4.7, fixed in Pipeline Integrity Monitor 2025 SP1 P2. None is reported as exploited. - Schneider Electric and Siemens ProductCERT September security advisories (incl. SSA-142885) and CISA ICSA-26-253-01 — round-up via SecurityWeek - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An APT cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm and a ransomware operator that deployed Qilin are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the control your USCG facility plan depends on
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and obtains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco shipped a fix in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, but only disclosed active exploitation on 9 September, saying it had observed attacks from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog on 9 September with a 12 September federal remediation deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters exploiting this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316 (KEV since 29 July, with known ransomware use): UAT-12197, unattributed, used CVE-2026-20079 to deploy a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws and whose tooling overlaps with Sandworm, deployed a Cyclops Blink variant; and UAT-11988, a ransomware operator that got in through CVE-2026-20316 alone and ultimately deployed Qilin. Ports and terminals should read this as a boundary problem. Network segregation between administrative systems and crane, gate, reefer and bunkering networks is a load-bearing control in USCG facility security and cyber plans, and FMC is where that segregation is defined. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; re-checked 11 Sep 2026 — no change of state reported

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms the MikroTik “MikroTrick” chain is being exploited — the router class that quietly carries port and berth connectivity
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerability chain known as “MikroTrick” — previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited — is now being used in real-world attacks, observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure and denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. This is a change of state, not a new vulnerability: the flaws were already known, and what is new is confirmed exploitation. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. Nothing ties this activity to a port, terminal or vessel operator. The reason it belongs on a maritime board is deployment pattern rather than targeting: low-cost RouterOS gear is a common choice for berth and yard wireless backhaul, remote-gate and weighbridge links, CCTV and reefer-monitoring segments, crew-welfare and contractor networks, and the small port-authority sites that sit outside the main terminal firewall estate — often installed by a contractor, rarely inventoried, and frequently reachable from the internet for support. - CERT Polska alert of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by Industrial Cyber - Exploitation confirmed 9 Sep 2026; activity observed from 2 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 12 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC warns exploitation of two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws is imminent — the gateway your shoreside support comes through
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre warned, in reporting published 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation attempts against two critical Check Point VPN vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both rated CVSS 9.8. The pair can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can additionally affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. This is an assessment, not an observation: no exploitation has been confirmed and no public exploit code had been reported at the time of the warning. It earns a place on a maritime board because of the role these gateways play either side of the quay. Ashore, they terminate the terminal operating system’s links to customs, shipping lines and haulier portals, and the vendor tunnels that reach crane, gate and reefer systems. Afloat, VPN concentrators fronting satellite links are how OEMs reach propulsion, power-management and navigation equipment for remote diagnostics. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer. Assessed as imminent; no confirmed exploitation and no maritime victims named - Check Point fixes released 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV, including the remote-support tool crane and TOS vendors log in with
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 and 11 September after evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to gain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors, while ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain carried separately here. For a terminal or port authority the ScreenConnect item is the one worth acting on: remote-support agents are how crane, gate, weighbridge, reefer-monitoring and terminal-operating-system vendors reach equipment out on the quay, and they are usually installed at commissioning by a contractor and never revisited. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV additions 10 Sep (RouterOS) and 11 Sep 2026 (ScreenConnect, Artifactory); reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your terminal’s IT provider runs — N-able N-central leads CISA’s 8 September KEV batch
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The one that matters most to ports and terminals is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code injection flaw scored CVSS 10.0 that gives pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild; Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform, which means an agent with system-level rights on managed endpoints. Many terminals, port authorities and smaller vessel-management companies outsource shoreside IT to an MSP running exactly this kind of console. Also added: two Windows zero-days granting SYSTEM (CVE-2026-81963, CVE-2026-85880) and an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw at CVSS 10.0. The federal remediation deadline is 11 September. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able and Huntress reporting — corroborated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; vendor hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch reaches vendor remote access and the firmware tool — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
item.description: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three matter for terminals and vessel operators. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — the pattern behind most crane, gate and terminal-automation support contracts. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH is the firmware tool for the controllers behind ship-to-shore cranes, conveyors and shore-power systems. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — Ignition turns up as the visualisation layer in terminal operating environments. None is reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition) - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos - Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition and the PaperCut security bulletin — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and The Hacker News - Vendor disclosed active exploitation 27 Aug 2026; CVEs assigned 28 Aug 2026; added to KEV 31 Aug 2026; post-exploitation activity reported by Arctic Wolf 6 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA refreshed the iDirect VSAT advisory on 10 September — the flaws are July’s, and the terminals are still on the vessel
item.category: Advisory — Shipboard VSAT terminal, advisory updated in-window
item.description: Be precise about what moved this week. CISA advisory ICSA-26-183-01 was originally published on 2 July 2026 and was updated on 10 September; nothing new was discovered, and the update is the reason it appears here rather than any fresh finding. It covers ST Engineering iDirect Evolution iQ Series, 3315 Series and 9 Series satellite terminals up to firmware 4.5.2.1. CVE-2026-38059 is a missing-authentication flaw that exposes the terminal’s REST interface, including an identity endpoint, without a login — serial numbers, device identifiers and terminal private keys can be read by anyone who can reach it, rated CVSS 7.5 under v3 and 8.7 under v4. CVE-2026-38057 is a cross-site request forgery against the reboot endpoint allowing a remote denial of service, rated CVSS 8.1 under v3 and 7.0 under v4. The fix is firmware 4.5.2.2 or later, and no exploitation has been confirmed. What makes this a fleet problem rather than a patch item is the position of the device. The VSAT terminal is usually the vessel’s only link, and the same path carries chart and route updates, engine and cargo telemetry, safety-management traffic, crew welfare and, in most modern arrangements, the shoreside remote support OEMs use to reach machinery systems. A reboot loop takes all of that at once, at sea, with no local engineer. And a leaked terminal private key is a different kind of loss again — it is a credential, so installing firmware does not retire it. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-183-01, republishing ST Engineering iDirect guidance — advisory update noted in OT security reporting of 11 Sep 2026 - Originally disclosed 2 Jul 2026; CISA advisory updated 10 Sep 2026 — the update introduced no new vulnerability

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, needing no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In maritime organisations NetScaler commonly fronts the remote access used by shoreside staff, crewing and technical departments, and by the OEMs who support engine, cargo and automation systems on vessels. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor patches released August 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026; continued exploitation reported 5 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s cyber decoys guide is aimed squarely at networks you are not allowed to change
item.category: Guidance — CISA detection and response
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September, a guide for critical infrastructure owners on deploying decoys, honeytokens and tripwires. It defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, detect their presence and support threat-intelligence collection, and it structures the work in three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — positioned alongside zero trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it matters for maritime is the constraint it works within. Terminal and shipboard networks are the environments where agents cannot be installed, protocols cannot be probed and a scanner is a genuine operational risk, which is why detection coverage there tends to lag the corporate estate by years. A decoy adds nothing to a production controller and touches no cargo or navigation process, but it produces a high-confidence alert the moment someone is enumerating a network they should not be on. This is guidance, not an advisory: there is no CVE, no product and no exploitation associated with it. - CISA guide “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reporting via SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Shipowners, ports and terminals are not the regulated party, but the vendors of navigation, cargo, crane and bridge equipment sold into the EU are, and IACS UR E26/E27 evidence expectations sit alongside this neatly. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — bridge and engine-room equipment makers now have 24 hours
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with exploit and mitigation detail, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix being available, as well as informing affected users. The regime applies to manufacturers placing products on the EU market wherever they are based, with penalties up to €15 million. For shipowners, managers and terminals this sits alongside rather than inside the IMO, IACS and USCG framework: it does not change what you must report, but it changes what your suppliers must tell you and when. Navigation, propulsion-control, power-management, AIS, ECDIS and terminal-automation vendors selling into Europe are now on a 24-hour clock. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal incident-reporting rules across 27 agencies — and a maritime operator can be inside several of them at once
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on GAO work, counting 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: duplicative filings with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same handful of people off containment during the first hours of an incident. Maritime is a clear example of the overlap. A single event at a US-flagged vessel or an MTSA-regulated facility can trigger reporting to the National Response Center under 33 CFR 101 Subpart F, a Coast Guard Captain of the Port notification, and, once CIRCIA rules are finalised — expected this autumn — a separate CISA filing, on top of any flag-state, class or charterer obligation. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO findings — via Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and the G7 tell operators to start the post-quantum inventory now — the deadline is set by your asset lifetimes, not by them
item.category: Guidance — CISA and G7 joint call to begin the post-quantum cryptography transition; no deadline attached
item.description: CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group issued a joint call on 4 September for governments and organisations to begin the transition to post-quantum cryptography, setting out a phased, risk-based approach: inventory the cryptography in use and the dependencies that carry it, identify the data and systems whose exposure would outlast the migration, and hold a written transition plan rather than a procurement wish. The statement is explicit about store-now-decrypt-later — traffic captured today can be decrypted later — and about the second-order problem, which is that authentication and firmware-signing chains rest on the same public-key algorithms. It is guidance, not a rule, and no deadline attaches. The relevance to maritime is asset lifetime: a vessel or terminal control system commissioned now will still be running in the 2040s, and the cryptography inside its firmware-signing and remote-access chains is being chosen today. - Joint statement from CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group, reported by Industrial Cyber - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical-infrastructure operators — terms not yet published
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry initiative
item.description: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For ports, terminals and shipping lines the relevance is indirect but real: maritime security spending is usually set against a compliance calendar rather than a threat one, and subsidised capability changes what a mid-sized terminal operator can put in front of a terminal operating system without first winning a business case. Note it, wait for the eligibility terms, and when they arrive read them as you would any third-party arrangement touching vessel or terminal operational data — the Coast Guard’s new policy office is likely to have a view on where that data sits. - SecurityWeek reporting on OpenAI’s Daybreak announcement - Announced and reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and terminals sit on both sides of it
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It calls for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Maritime is a good test case: when North Carolina Ports moved to manual cargo processing in early August, the operational question for every carrier, drayage firm and shipper on the other side was simply what to expect and for how long. A terminal is a service provider to that chain, and the guidance is written for exactly that position. - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and CISA — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Proposed, not yet in force
item.description: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage. - SecurityWeek reporting on the amendments tabled to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; not yet in force — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — expect the inspections to sharpen
item.category: Regulation — US Coast Guard maritime cyber governance
item.description: The US Coast Guard has stood up the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) as the central authority for cybersecurity policy covering ports, vessels and facilities across the Marine Transportation System, reporting to the Director of Inspections and Compliance. Its remit is to write policy, run a unified compliance strategy, coordinate enforcement and industry engagement, and track emerging technology and cyber risk. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings about gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight. Nothing in the MTS cyber rule changes today, but the practical effect of consolidating policy and compliance under one office is usually consistency: the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities. - US Coast Guard ALCOAST 266/26 and Coast Guard news release — corroborated by ExecutiveGov and Industrial Cyber - Office establishment announced Aug 2026; reported 1 Sep 2026
